en.title: 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act
en.excerpt: A wide-ranging federal bill to increase the supply of housing nationwide. It expands financing for affordable housing, funds local planning and community-development grants, streamlines federal environmental review for qualifying projects, modernizes manufactured- and modular-housing rules, reforms the HOME and rural-housing programs, and tightens oversight of HUD and public housing agencies. Introduced December 2025, it passed the House 390–9 and the Senate 89–10; the CBO found it would not increase the federal deficit.
en.summary: The 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act is a wide-ranging federal bill whose stated purpose is to increase the supply of housing in America by modernizing outdated programs, removing unnecessary federal requirements, and increasing local flexibility. It spans six titles and 38 sections covering housing finance, manufactured housing, rural programs, environmental review, and oversight.
en.methodNote: This review applies the Center's four-stage method: we decompose the bill into testable provisions, match each to comparable enacted policy from the past fifty years, trace how those precedents actually fared, and project the likely outcome with explicit confidence.

provisions.title: Streamlined federal review
provisions.body: Exempts qualifying residential construction, rehabilitation, and improvement from certain NEPA review requirements.

provisions.title: Manufactured & modular modernization
provisions.body: Eliminates the permanent-chassis requirement and updates standards to expand factory-built supply.

provisions.title: Expanded affordable-housing finance
provisions.body: Raises multifamily loan limits and reforms the HOME Investment Partnerships program.

provisions.title: Planning & development grants
provisions.body: Funds local planning, zoning modernization, and implementation tied to affordable-housing production.

provisions.title: Rural Housing Service reform
provisions.body: Modernizes USDA rural housing programs and strengthens interagency coordination.

provisions.title: HUD & PHA accountability
provisions.body: Requires public contract disclosure, performance reviews, and regular regulator testimony.

precedents.title: The Supply Response to Zoning Reform (Minneapolis 2040)
precedents.finding: Permitted units rose ~12% over four years — measurable but lagged and spatially uneven.

precedents.title: Minimum Lot Size Reform and Housing Production
precedents.finding: Per-unit land costs fell ~18% where prior minimums were most binding.

precedents.title: Land-Use Deregulation and Regional Housing Affordability
precedents.finding: Metro-scale liberalization eased rents modestly, with multi-year lags.

precedents.title: Inclusionary Zoning and Market-Rate Production
precedents.finding: Net effect on starts depends heavily on the stringency of the set-aside.

effects.label: Onset
effects.body: Permitting responses to land-use and review reform typically appear within 1–2 years; completed units lag 3–5 years behind, constrained by financing and construction.

effects.label: Magnitude
effects.body: Comparable reforms raised permitted supply on the order of 10–18% in affected areas — largest where prior regulation was most binding.

effects.label: Persistence
effects.body: Supply gains generally persisted where reforms were durable; rent and affordability effects were smaller, slower, and contingent on a sustained supply response.

effects.label: Distribution
effects.body: Effects were spatially uneven — concentrated in higher-amenity, higher-land-value areas and muted in low-income peripheries.

outlook.headline: Moderate positive supply effect
outlook.body: Likely to raise housing supply over a 2–5 year horizon, with smaller and slower effects on rents.

en.aiNote: The strongest evidentiary support is for the land-use and review-streamlining provisions, which mirror the Minneapolis 2040 and lot-size reforms. The manufactured-housing modernization has thinner domestic precedent and is rated lower-confidence. Net affordability effects are likely small in the near term and depend on a sustained supply response.

reviews.name: Dr. Dana Okonkwo
reviews.text: The precedent matching is sound. The supply provisions are well-supported by the Minneapolis and lot-size evidence, and the affordability projection is appropriately cautious.

reviews.name: Dr. Kwame Mills
reviews.text: The manufactured-housing provisions lack a strong domestic precedent; the moderate-confidence rating is warranted. I would flag implementation risk more explicitly.

reviews.name: Dr. Lan Tran
reviews.text: Environmental-review streamlining is the highest-leverage provision, and the projected multi-year horizon is realistic given entitlement lags.
